reasons_add: Al-Ghazālī reads the Fātiḥa’s repeated mercy language as encompassing perfect creation and provision in each world as well as mercy in the afterlife.
Biqāʿī associates al-Raḥmān with lordship in both creations and al-Raḥīm especially with the second creation, preservation, recompense, and special mercy.
Abū Hurayra's reports also include the title the Magnificent Qurʾān among the Prophet's names for al-Fātiḥa.
Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the companions accepted sheep after the bitten or stung man recovered; the Prophet expressly approved payment for healing by recitation of God's Book.
ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jābir also transmits the Prophet's description of al-Fātiḥa as the best revealed sūra.
The narrator of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jābir's report is unsure whether the Prophet also called al-Fātiḥa a cure for every illness.
Abū Salmān adds that the companions recited al-Fātiḥa into the ear of the man suffering a seizure; the Prophet identified it as the Mother of the Book.
Kharija ibn al-Ṣalt's report specifies recitation morning and evening for three days and a payment of one hundred sheep; its wording identifies Kharija as the reciter.

question: 1:1/q57
position: Ibn Masʿūd was the first after the Prophet to recite the Qurʾān publicly in Mecca; Quraysh beat him, but he was ready to repeat it.
reasons: ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr reports Ibn Masʿūd's public recitation, the beating by Quraysh, and his resolve to recite again.
